title: Every Upper-Lower Spelling
statement:
You get a string s made of English letters and digits. Each letter may be written in lowercase or in uppercase; digits stay as they are.

Return every string you can get this way, each exactly once. The strings may be returned in any order.

examples.why: Two letters, two choices each: 4 strings. The digit never changes.
An uppercase letter in the input can be lowered too.
No letters, so the only result is the string itself.

constraints: s contains only English letters and digits
hints: Walk the string from left to right. A digit gives one way forward; a letter gives two.
That is a binary decision tree with one level per letter. Each root-to-leaf path is one answer.
Either backtrack (choose lower, recurse, choose upper, recurse), or build the list level by level: for every letter, double the list by adding both cases to each partial string.

explain.intuition:
Every letter is an independent yes/no choice: lower or upper. With L letters there are exactly 2^L results, and no two coincide, because they differ in the case of some letter. So the job is to walk the decision tree and emit each leaf.

Backtracking does it with one shared character buffer: set position i to the lowercase letter, recurse, set it to uppercase, recurse. Digits skip straight to the next position. An equivalent iterative version starts from [""] and, for each character, extends every partial string by one or two characters.
steps: Copy s into a character array and start at index 0.
If the index reaches the end, push the joined string.
If the character is a digit, move to the next index.
If it is a letter, set it to lowercase and recurse, then set it to uppercase and recurse.
pitfalls: Only toggling the case of a letter instead of trying both: you miss the original spelling or emit it twice.
Branching on digits too, which produces duplicate strings.
Assuming the input letters are lowercase. "7Z" must still produce "7z".

solutions.title: Grow the list character by character
solutions.idea: Start from [""]; for each character extend every partial string, doubling the list at letters.

solutions.title: Backtracking over one buffer
solutions.idea: At each letter try lowercase, recurse, then uppercase, recurse.

solutions.title: Bitmask over the letters
solutions.idea: Number the letters 0 … L − 1; each mask from 0 to 2^L − 1 says which ones are uppercase.

followups: Return the results in sorted order without sorting at the end.
Instead of listing them, return only the k-th spelling in the order the bitmask version produces.
